item.title: The second wheel Bangladesh keeps ignoring. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On factory floors across Bangladesh right now, workers are welding frames that will never touch a sewing machine. What leaves those gates does not stitch anyone a shirt. It rolls out on two wheels, bound for Hamburg or Vienna. Nobody outside the industry notices them much. Perhaps they should.
Bangladesh's economy still speaks one language to the world. Garments alone brought in 84% of the country's export earnings last fiscal year , according to figures the commerce minister placed before parliament this June. A nation of 170 million people has built its entire trading identity around a needle and thread. That comfort has served us for four decades. It will not serve us for the next one.
There is a smaller story here that sits quietly beside the big one that needs a closer look. Quite remarkably, Bangladesh made a handsome $ 116.44 million from bicycle exports in fiscal year 2024/25 . This is a skyrocketed figure with a jump of 4% over the year before . Germany alone bought $34.39m worth of Bangladeshi bicycles. Eurostat now places Bangladesh as the third largest bicycle supplier to the European Union and the eighth largest in the world.
What makes the recovery worth watching is how it happened. Exports had touched $ 168m during the pandemic cycling rush , then fell by half once European retailers worked through their overstock and the war in Ukraine cooled demand further.
Plenty of export sectors never climb back after a fall like that. Bangladesh's bicycle makers did climb back, and that says more about the industry's staying power than any single good year could.
Europe is also moving in a direction that suits us. The European Cyclists' Federation expects the continent to sell 30 million bicycles a year by 2030 , close to 10 million more than today, driven by city planners redesigning streets and younger buyers choosing bikes over cars, not because of fashion.
There is a policy tailwind working in our favour too. The European Commission renewed its anti-dumping duties on Chinese bicycles in January 2025, this time extending the measure to cover electric bicycles as well . Brussels did more for Bangladeshi exporters with that single decision than most of our domestic industrial policy combined.
Here is where the celebration needs a pause. Protections handed down by someone else's trade ruling are never permanent. They come up for review.
Politics in Brussels can shift. And a much larger deadline is already bearing down on us. Bangladesh was to graduate from least developed country status on November 24, 2026 , though the government has now asked the United Nations to push that date to 2029 .
Whichever date holds, the World Trade Organization has warned Bangladesh could lose close to $8bn a year in export earnings once current trade preferences run out, while UNCTAD's own estimate runs as high as $17.5bn.
Most of that exposure sits with garments. It should still worry the bicycle industry, because a weakness sits right at its centre that nobody has fixed.
Bangladesh still imports the bulk of the expensive parts that go into every bicycle it exports. Annual demand for freewheels and sprockets alone runs to roughly 35 to 40 lakh and 50 to 55 lakh units, most of it met through imports, even though the Trade and Tariff Commission found local value addition in these parts already running close to 40% .
Every imported gear and chain raises our own production cost and sends the margin straight back to a foreign supplier. Garments could survive on imported fabric because labour was cheap enough to absorb the loss. Bicycles cannot lean on the same trick.
We have solved a version of this problem before. When motorcycle assemblers faced the identical bottleneck a decade ago, the government cut the duty on completely knocked down units by 25 percentage points in 2016 .
Within a few years, local manufacturing and assembly met 96% of domestic motorcycle demand instead of relying on imports for nearly all of it. Nobody had to invent a new economic model. A tariff structure changed, and investors responded.
The same tools sit within reach for bicycles. Lower duties on components would encourage local vendors to enter the space rather than depend on imports. Bonded warehouse access, already extended to garment factories, could be widened to cover bicycle component manufacturers as well.
Trade diplomacy with Brussels needs to begin now, while the graduation date is still being negotiated, not after the clock runs out and our negotiating position weakens.
Bangladesh has already shown twice that it can win foreign buyers on quality rather than cheap labour alone. Garments proved it first. Bicycles are proving it again, on a smaller scale but a genuine one.
The choice in front of us is whether we treat this as a pleasant accident or as a pillar our economy has needed since long before anyone in Frankfurt noticed our welders.
We built one industry because building two felt unnecessary. That comfort is running out of road faster than we think. Bicycles alone will not carry an economy of 170 million people. But they are proof that we can compete on something other than a sewing machine, provided we invest in the parts before the deadline arrives, not after.
Nazma Sultana holds a key strategic position at Akij Bicycle & Engineering Limited (ABEL).

item.title: The missing gratitude for thankless jobs. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The desk lamp in a newsroom in Dhaka flickers at 2:00 AM, casting long, fatigued shadows across pages of investigative drafts, while a weary educator in a rural government primary school in Kurigram corrects her 400th exam paper by the dim glow of a mobile phone torch.
Down the street, a municipal sanitation worker clears choked drains before dawn, unseen and unacknowledged by the waking city.
In the architecture of modern civilization, certain labour operates like the foundation of a building -- buried deep underground, taking the crushing weight of the entire structure, yet entirely forgotten until something breaks.
These are the thankless jobs.
Within the specific and high-stakes context of Bangladesh, the phrase "thankless job" takes on a sharp, almost harrowing edge.
To understand what truly constitutes a thankless job, we must look beyond the mere absence of praise.
A genuinely thankless job is defined by a paradox: Its practitioners bear the immense burden of sustaining societal truth, social mobility, and public health, yet they are systematically met with suspicion, ridicule, intimidation, and prosecution at whim.
What makes a job truly thankless? It is not merely low pay -- though financial precarity is almost always a faithful companion. Rather, it is the fundamental asymmetry between the liability one carries and the dignity one is afforded.
The journalist: Walking a tightrope of peril
Consider the journalist, particularly within the sociopolitical landscape of Bangladesh.
Journalism is ostensibly framed as the "fourth estate," a pillar of democracy. In reality, practicing independent journalism here often feels like walking a tightrope over an active volcano.
When a reporter uncovers systemic corruption in public procurement, financial sector anomalies, or bureaucratic inertia, the immediate reaction from the powerful is rarely introspection or reform.
Instead, it is a knee-jerk defense mechanism characterized by hostility. Journalists are routinely questioned, ridiculed in public forums, intimidated by non-state actors, and prosecuted under draconian legal instruments -- such as legacy cyber-security or digital safety laws that weaponize ambiguity against the press.
The public consumes the news with morning tea, often criticizing the media for being "biased" or "sensationalist," while remaining entirely insulated from the physical threats, midnight summons, and psychological toll borne by reporters in district towns and metropolitan hubs alike.
The journalist labours under a relentless cloud of hostility, where doing the job correctly makes you an enemy of those you hold accountable.
The frontline pillars
This dynamic extends far beyond the newsroom.
A thankless job, therefore, is one where society demands perfection, absorbs the immense value produced, and repays the worker with vulnerability, disrespect, and peril.
Why thankless jobs are the cogs of societal survival
It is easy to dismiss these professions as unfortunate casualties of economic inequality.
However, a deeper sociological examination reveals a chilling truth: Society runs smoothly precisely because these jobs are thankless.
The structural thanklessness of these roles is often the mechanism by which power dynamics are maintained and societal friction is absorbed. Without them, the veneer of order collapses.
To understand why the thankless job of the journalist is non-negotiable for a functioning society, we can look at a journalistic anecdote.
In the early 2020s, local investigative reports in regional Bangladeshi newspapers highlighted how syndicates were artificially inflating prices of essential commodities at local haats (traditional markets) through cartelization.
The journalists who broke these stories faced intense local pressure, threats of physical assault from local political muscle, and frivolous defamation lawsuits designed to bankrupt them legally.
Why did powerful vested interests react with such venom? Because journalism acts as society’s immune system.
When a pathogen (corruption, abuse of power, systemic theft) enters the body politic, the immune system attacks it. This process is inherently inflammatory and painful.
If journalists were thanked, coddled, and protected by the establishment, it would mean the establishment welcomed self-correction. But power rarely welcomes correction.
By making journalism thankless, a society attempts to suppress its own immune response.
Yet, without that painful, thankless reporting, the socioeconomic body rots from within.
Unchecked corruption drains national reserves, banking sectors hollow out, and inflation crushes the working class.
The journalist's thankless persistence is the only barrier preventing total systemic opacity.
Similarly, the thankless labour of the teacher is the glue holding social mobility together. In a developing economy like Bangladesh, education is the primary elevator out of intergenerational poverty.
When teachers in under-resourced classrooms dedicate their evenings to counseling struggling students or managing massive administrative burdens without adequate support, they are quietly absorbing the failures of the state's social welfare apparatus.
If teaching were truly valued and supported commensurate with its actual impact, resource allocation would shift dramatically.
By keeping the profession underpaid, overworked, and structurally unappreciated, the system manages to extract maximum emotional and intellectual labour at minimal cost -- treating educators as martyrs of necessity rather than professionals of value.
The Bangladeshi context and the path forward
In Bangladesh, the cultural narrative surrounding labour is often tied to visible, tangible production -- garments manufactured, bridges built, remittances sent from the Middle East.
These are celebrated, and rightly so; they drive the macroeconomic indicators.
However, the invisible labour -- the journalistic truth-telling, the foundational teaching, the municipal sanitation -- operates in the cultural blind spot.
We celebrate the ribbon-cuttings of mega-infrastructure projects, but we rarely protect or thank the journalists who investigate the structural integrity of those projects, nor the low-tier engineers and supervisors who blow the whistle on substandard materials at personal risk.
When we punish or ignore those in thankless jobs, we induce a profound societal brain drain and moral apathy.
Talented youth steer clear of investigative journalism, public school teaching, and civil rights advocacy, preferring safer, more lucrative corporate or bureaucratic tracks where compliance is rewarded over conscience.
A society that consumes the fruits of a thankless job while starving, intimidating, or prosecuting the tree-tender is borrowing prosperity from its own future.
True reform in Bangladesh requires a cultural and structural pivot. It demands legal safeguards that protect journalists from arbitrary prosecution, fair compensation and social prestige for educators, and basic human dignity for frontline workers.
Until we recognize that the health of a nation is measured not just by its tall buildings and export volumes, but by how it treats those who bear its heaviest and most unrewarded crosses, our progress will remain fragile -- built on the exhausted backs of those we refuse to thank.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: PCB releases Sufiyan Moqim from tri-series squad, adds Maaz Sadaqat as cover. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Sunday released left-arm wrist spinner Sufiyan Moqim from the national men’s squad for the ongoing One-day International tri-series involving England and Sri Lanka, citing the nature of the pitches in Lahore, while adding left-handed batter Maaz Sadaqat as cover for players carrying minor niggles.

In a brief statement, the PCB said Sufiyan had been released from the squad “keeping in view the nature of Lahore pitches” and would return to domestic cricket. Maaz, meanwhile, had been added as cover for players with minor niggles.

The move comes as the tri-series shifts to the Gaddafi Stadium after the opening three matches in Rawalpindi. Pakistan have won both their league games so far, beating Sri Lanka by 37 runs and England by 87, and face England again in Lahore on Sunday. The pitches in Rawalpindi generally favoured pace, limiting opportunities for specialist spinners.

Sufiyan, who hails from Azad Kashmir, has represented Pakistan in limited-overs cricket since making his T20I debut in 2023. He is best known for his record-equalling figures of five for three against Zimbabwe in a T20 International and was named Player of the Tournament in the 2026 Pakistan Super League while playing for Peshawar Zalmi. In ODIs, he has taken eight wickets in four matches.

Maaz, 21, has attracted attention with his aggressive batting. The Peshawar-born left-hander made an immediate impact on his ODI debut against Bangladesh earlier this year and recently impressed in the T20I series against Sri Lanka, scoring consecutive half-centuries, including a blistering 96 off 51 balls that helped Pakistan post their highest T20I total at home.

An occasional left-arm orthodox spinner, Maaz had initially been left out of the tri-series squad.

The updated squad, led by Shaheen Shah Afridi, now includes Maaz as Pakistan continue their campaign in Lahore ahead of the final on Oct 31 at the same venue.

item.title: Where is the justice?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There's an old saying that all of economics is either footnotes to Adam Smith or wrong.
Like most old sayings, it's not wholly and exactly correct but there is still a great deal of truth in it.
For one of the reasons that old sayings survive is that people note there's a lot of truth in there and so keep repeating it.
That we've still got the saying can thus be a proof that there's a useful amount of truth in it.
With that in mind, we can discuss the disaster that is this news : “Bangladesh ranked 123rd among 143 countries and jurisdictions in the World Justice Project (WJP) index” and justice here is referring to things like corruption, regulatory enforcement, and so on, eight areas in total.
The one that concerns us here is “civil justice was the second-weakest area, with Bangladesh ranking 132nd and scoring 0.36.”
We know about corruption, about the ineffectiveness of regulatory enforcement, and so on. But thieves and incompetence we also don't want. The effectiveness -- or not -- of civil justice is one of those things not enough people think about enough of the time.
Adam Smith did point out that “little else is requisite to carry a state to the highest degree of opulence from the lowest barbarism but peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice: All the rest being brought about by the natural course of things.”
Peace we're all doing pretty well on in this corner of the world. Easy taxes could be easier but the Bangladeshi state does not swallow an inordinate amount of everyone's production or work.
Which leaves us that administration of justice.
Given that we are talking about the economy here, it's that part of justice associated with the economy that matters to us.
The ability to go to court and get as the contract enforced -- say. Which is, as we know, a wholly laughable proposition in the Bangladeshi courts of today. Which is, therefore, the thing that needs to be fixed.
We can also borrow something from our other ideas about the economy. That, in business at least, it is often better to make a fast decision than delay and then, perhaps, make the right one.
Borrowing that idea means that the law, about contracts and commerce, needs to be fast. It's better that it be fast than it be wholly just or near perfect.
A decision -- even, sometimes the wrong one -- given now is better than grinding through the process for another five years.
Something that will be anathema to the lawyers of course, they get paid by the hour, but still true all the same.
It would be even better if we always got the right decisions -- but let's do this step by step. We need commercial law -- that part of civil justice which works with business and the economy -- to be swift.
We also need it to be certain. If the contract says something, it must be definitive. The same is true for the law -- that's what the decision will be.
Those decisions need to come quickly. These two conditions are more important than grinding through to a decision in a decade.
It's not wholly true that Adam Smith was correct about everything he discussed but it's still a remarkably good basis to start our reasoning from. As he points out, there are things that governments really do have to do in order to ensure that the economy grows.
One of these is a commercial legal system that actually works. And by works, we mean swift and certain decisions more than necessarily wholly fair or even correct ones.
As the World Justice Project's index points out, this is something Bangladesh is failing upon and failing badly. We should correct that error.
We all know that it's going to take years, if not decades, to recover the money from those who looted the banks last decade. If nothing else about efficient justice, it would be nice to bankrupt the thieves before they die, no? You know, the tolerable administration of justice.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Weaponizing humiliation. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Perhaps there is no such thing as privacy in Bangladesh. Even where it exists, many in the authorities or the media do not understand what it means. Even if they do understand, they are unwilling to act according to the essence of privacy.
This unwillingness is strongest when an opportunity arises to violate a woman’s privacy. Society has still not found any way to suppress the urge to humiliate women in public.
Last Tuesday, personnel of the detective branch raided the residence of an Additional DIG of police in Purbachal, near Dhaka. It was described as an anti-narcotics operation (though these days even a raid on a club or bar is called an “anti-narcotics operation”). But there did not seem to be much presence of drugs there.
In the photos released, although there was a bottle and a half of liquor, the absence of narcotics was noticeable. However, that is not the problem with this operation. The question is about the way the operation was publicized in the media, or the way arrangements were made to publicize it.
Some days ago, during a police raid on a club called German Club in Dhaka, the entire scene was being filmed from outside the main gate. As the club’s guests came out one by one, they were filmed, and the video was spread on social media, with one particular woman going viral on social media.
But what happened in Purbachal was even more disgraceful, and here it was not only the unbridled content creators of social media, but even established mainstream news media that got involved.
Videos were shot inside the Purbachal house, in various rooms. When several girls came down the stairs from the upper floor, one or two tried to cover their faces with their orna (scarf) while their faces were being filmed, but most could not.
The men present also appeared in the video, though the focus was mostly on the women. Hearing the description of the raid, many will assume that some “immoral activity” was going on there. And when, on top of that, one woman’s face after another appears in the video, no psychologist is needed to understand what picture forms in the public’s mind.
Here the question may be asked: Which is the immoral activity? Adult men and women socializing inside a home? Or is it the filming of women, calling the house a “harem,” and humiliating them socially?
By shooting and circulating the video, the women were not merely humiliated. They were humiliated knowingly and deliberately, and their safety was put at risk.
One thing needs to be made clear. It is normal for police to record videos in any operation. It is important to preserve through video information such as whether the operation is being conducted according to the police’s own rules, how and where evidence was found, and how and where the detainees were held.
But that video would be the police’s own evidence, meant to assist their own investigation, an important part of the process of collecting testimony and evidence against the accused.
Such a video will play an important role in framing formal charges and conducting the case. Similarly, the accused’s lawyers can use these same police videos to try to get the allegations against their client dismissed. But the videos of the recent operations do not seem to have been taken to assist a case.
First, it is not clear who shot the videos. At least from the video taken outside the gate of German Club, it seemed that it was no one from the police. That is, someone who got news of the raid went there and filmed it.
Is the Purbachal incident the same? The videos were taken both inside and outside the house. One woman was seen pointing a finger at the person filming and saying something. Had someone from the police been holding the camera, that woman would perhaps not have done so.
The most disgraceful thing was spreading those videos on social media, exposing the women’s faces, and humiliating them in public.
Such an incident, while not common, once again begs the question of ethics in a section of the country’s media. Law enforcement agencies also have a big role in building this habit.
For many years, the police, and later RAB or BGB, have been supplying the media with photos and identities of people detained on charges of some alleged crime.
Even when the detainee was only a suspect, his photo was given to the media, often with a signboard calling him a criminal hung around his neck. This still happens.
That a person is innocent until proven guilty in court, this fundamental principle of law seems to be unknown to Bangladesh’s law enforcement agencies.
The Bangladeshi media industry too has never quite had anything in the way of editorial policy or ethical standards. Some large organizations have discussed ethics and, in some cases, tried to create a policy of their own.
For example, at one time the photos and identities of women who were victims of rape used to be printed. But that has changed. The identity of victims is now kept secret in most cases.
But the accused also deserve this kind of protection. Formal charges can be framed against someone only when there is sufficient evidence, and until charges are framed, the identity of the accused should also be kept secret.
Even now, photos of accused or suspected persons provided by the police are being published along with their identities. As for social media content creators, that is a separate matter, and it is doubtful whether there is any editorial vetting in their work.
In many cases, such creators run a channel single-handedly, and they depend entirely on view counts and engagement for income. They do not have time to worry about editorial “decency” or ethical considerations.
Established mainstream media is a different matter. They have staff and the capacity to read and think about what has been done in other countries of the world on journalistic rules, editorial policy, ethics, and so on.
It is possible for them to create their own policies on how to report while protecting the rights, privacy, and safety of ordinary people, and to give journalists the necessary training on these matters.
In particular, established media can sensitize journalists on how to cover delicate stories involving women, children, religious or ethnic minorities, and other vulnerable groups.
This work should have been done long ago. But even now, photos, names, and identities of detainees provided by the police are still being published.
The media needs to think about how their reporting can harm ordinary people. Care must be taken so that people who are innocent in the eyes of the law are not declared “guilty” in a media trial and socially humiliated.
Humiliating those who have no power, who are not wealthy, who have no connections in high circles, and who have no influential mama-chacha in political circles is not merely wrong. It is quite literally another crime. This is especially so when women’s photos or videos are being published with no regard for their social dignity and safety.
Just as initiative is needed from the media industry to stop this practice, the government also needs to impose restrictions on the police so that they do not do anything that could humiliate people before a trial in court.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Nothing is more important than protecting our children. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The recurring reports of physical and sexual abuse of children within educational institutions across the country lay bare what can only be termed a horrifying national failure.
When schools, madrasas, and learning centres - places meant to nurture and protect our nation’s youth - become sites of predatory violence and terror, the foundational contract between society and the state is shattered.
Recent alarms raised by child rights advocates regarding abuse cases expose a pervasive, systemic rot that can no longer be ignored or swept under the rug with bureaucratic platitudes.
For too long, child protection in Bangladesh has been undermined by a culture of silence, social stigma, and institutional cover-ups. Predators are allowed to operate with virtual impunity, exploiting power imbalances to silence vulnerable victims through threats and intimidation.
When children are forced to choose between their education and their personal safety, the institutional framework entrusted with their welfare has utterly collapsed.
Protecting children cannot remain a rhetorical talking point for NGOs and press releases. The government must immediately enforce rigorous, binding child-protection protocols across every educational institution nationwide, without exception.
Allegations of abuse must be met with swift, impartial criminal investigation, prosecution, and absolute accountability, stripping away the impunity enjoyed by so many perpetrators.
Educational authorities too must do their part by establishing secure, confidential reporting channels and robust psychosocial support systems, ensuring that victims and their families are believed, protected, and prioritized.
A nation that fails to safeguard its children from predators within its own classrooms has forfeited its moral authority. We need to be getting rid of this rot with the urgency it warrants, ruthlessly purging abusive environments and transforming our schools and madrasas into genuine safe havens before more generations of children are scarred by institutional cowardice.

item.title: Logistical deficits not a good enough excuse for law enforcement. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There is no denying the grueling realities faced by ground-level law enforcement personnel in Bangladesh.
It cannot be easy to operate amid severe logistical deficits, including acute transport shortages and a lack of proper housing facilities, for nearly 90% of the force. Officers also often endure grueling 12-to-16-hour shifts under immense pressure.
This is a reality we must acknowledge, and we sympathize with those within the forces.
Equipping the force with necessary transport, housing, and operational backing is thus a vital administrative duty that the government must address without delay.
However, recognizing the genuine hardships of police work must never translate into a blanket excuse for systemic failure or poor public service.
The primary grievance of ordinary citizens with law enforcement agencies has been an entrenched culture of authoritarian intimidation and a callous disregard for public welfare.
Too often, the badge has been wielded as an instrument of power and coercion rather than protection, leaving communities alienated and terrified of the very institutions meant to secure them.
Logistical upgrades and multi-crore vehicle procurements will mean nothing if the internal ethos of the force remains rot-ridden.
A lack of transport does not excuse extortion at checkpoints, nor does substandard housing justify custodial abuse, bribery, or the routine weaponization of the law against the vulnerable.
For generations, citizens have been forced to navigate a police apparatus that views them with suspicion or contempt rather than dignity and service. For that to change, it will take more than overhauling institutional capacity.
Accountability must match investment step for step. Officers deserve fair working conditions and adequate resources, but the public deserves law enforcement agencies that genuinely care for and protect them.
